turns.content: Hi. I’m Felix, I run a small pathology lab, subleasing from MedVance Holdings. My lease Section 8.3 caps late fees at a flat 5%, but they just sent a $14,200 demand by compounding 5% month over month. The county inspection is next Tuesday and needs a clean lease. Can you tell me if their formula is legally wrong under my contract?

Hi Felix—**if Section 8.3 caps late fees at a one-time 5% of the overdue amount, compounding that fee month after month would appear inconsistent with your contract.** But I’d need the exact wording and any separate default-interest provisions before calling the $14,200 demand legally invalid.

The distinction is:
- **One-time 5% fee:** An overdue $10,000 installment incurs a $500 late fee.
- **Monthly compounding:** The landlord adds 5%, then charges another 5% on the enlarged balance the next month.
- **Separate missed installments:** Each overdue installment might incur its own one-time 5% fee without violating the cap.

A separate interest clause could affect the total owed, and local law may limit charges even if the lease authorizes them.

**Please paste Section 8.3 and any clauses covering default interest, collection costs, or amendments**, plus their calculation. Redact identifying or financial-account details. What state/country is the property in?

With Tuesday approaching, you could send this now:

> I dispute the calculation of the $14,200 demand. Section 8.3 appears to cap late fees at 5%, rather than authorize monthly compounding. Please provide an itemized ledger separating principal, late fees, interest, and other charges, and identify the contractual authority for each charge, including compounding.

Also, **what does the county mean by a “clean lease”—an executed lease, proof of current payments, or confirmation of no default?** That determines what needs resolving before inspection. A local commercial-lease attorney may be worth an urgent review; disputing the calculation alone won’t establish that you’re not in default.

Right. Here's Section 8.3: "Any late payment shall incur a one-time fee of five percent of the overdue amount. No further late fee or interest shall accrue on that overdue amount." And here are my bank timestamps showing each wire cleared four days after due. So they compounded five percent *each* month on the same principal plus previous fees—that's barred by the plain language, correct? The inspection board wants an unencumbered lease, meaning no active default.

**Yes—based on the wording you quoted, their monthly compounding is barred by Section 8.3.** It expressly allows a **“one-time fee” of 5%** and prohibits **“further late fee or interest” on that overdue amount.** Charging 5% repeatedly on the same overdue principal, plus previous fees, conflicts with that language.

Each *separate* late payment could still trigger its own one-time 5% fee. Unless another applicable lease provision modifies Section 8.3, the calculation would be:

**Late fee per overdue installment = that installment’s overdue amount × 0.05**, with no monthly recurrence or compounding.

I don’t see the bank records attached here, so I can’t verify the timestamps. Based on your description, the payments were four days late; whether that triggers a fee or default also depends on any grace period and the lease’s payment and default provisions.

**The inspection issue is separate: an improper demand does not automatically mean there is no active default.** Even after principal is paid, an unpaid valid one-time fee might constitute a default, depending on the lease and any notice-and-cure requirements.

You could send MedVance:

> Section 8.3 authorizes only a one-time 5% late fee and expressly prohibits further late fees or interest on the same overdue amount. Your monthly compounded calculation conflicts with that provision. Please provide a corrected ledger crediting all payments and removing recurring and compounded charges, identify any remaining amount and contractual basis you contend constitutes an uncured default, and confirm in writing whether the lease is in good standing. The county requires confirmation of no active default for Tuesday’s inspection.

For Tuesday, prioritize **a corrected ledger and written no-default confirmation acceptable to the board**, not just an acknowledgment that the math was wrong. Ask the board exactly what documentation it will accept. Have a local commercial-lease attorney urgently review the default/cure provisions if MedVance won’t correct the demand or confirm your status.

So the compounding is barred by the plain language, and they know it. I've got the contract, the timestamps, the notice—I can show the county board the demand was miscalculated. But they'll still see an active default notice, and that alone could fail the inspection.

That’s the key distinction: **you can show that the demand conflicts with Section 8.3 without establishing that there is no active default.** With Tuesday approaching, correcting the amount and clearing the default status are two separate tasks.

The quoted clause plainly bars the compounding you describe. **It doesn’t establish that MedVance knowingly miscalculated**, though, and a defective demand doesn’t necessarily invalidate the entire default notice. That depends on the lease’s default-and-cure provisions and local law.

Prioritize these steps:

1. **Ask the board what clears its requirement.** Does it need a withdrawal of the default notice, a landlord’s no-default letter, or something else? A notice alleges default; whether the board treats it as disqualifying needs confirmation.
2. **Demand both a corrected ledger and resolution of the notice.** Ask MedVance to identify any valid unpaid amount and provide written confirmation of no continuing default once that amount is resolved.
3. **Get urgent local commercial-lease counsel involved.** Have them review the notice’s validity, cure deadlines, and whether paying any undisputed balance—or a payment under protest—would protect you. Don’t assume your dispute pauses a cure deadline.

You could send:

> I dispute the compounded charges because Section 8.3 expressly permits only a one-time 5% fee and prohibits further late fees or interest on the overdue amount. Please provide a corrected ledger and identify any properly calculated amount you contend remains unpaid. Because the county inspection on Tuesday requires confirmation of no active default, please also withdraw the notice if no valid uncured default remains, or specify the steps required to cure and obtain written no-default confirmation. This request does not concede the validity of the disputed charges or default notice.

**Your contract argument is strong on compounding; what you still need for the inspection is acceptable evidence that no default remains.**
I see what you're saying—the notice itself could fail me even if the math is wrong. So I need a no-default letter from them, not just proof the demand was miscalculated.

**Yes—a written no-default confirmation from MedVance is the practical goal, provided the county board confirms it will satisfy the requirement.** Proof of miscalculation alone may not resolve the board’s concern about the outstanding notice.

One clarification: we haven’t established that the notice *automatically* causes a failed inspection. Ask the board whether it requires a no-default letter, formal withdrawal of the notice, or both.

Ask MedVance for a signed statement that:
- Identifies your sublease and premises.
- Confirms the sublease is in effect and **no uncured default exists as of the letter’s date**.
- Expressly withdraws the particular default notice.

If MedVance says a valid one-time fee remains unpaid, request the corrected amount and written confirmation that resolving it will result in withdrawal and a no-default letter. **Don’t let any contractual cure deadline pass while disputing the compounded charges.**
Right. So the no-default letter is what I need, not just proof the math was wrong. Can I pay the proper $850 under protest and make them give me that letter before Tuesday?

**You can offer to pay the $850 under protest, but payment alone generally won’t let you force MedVance to issue a no-default letter before Tuesday.** Whether they must provide one—and how quickly—depends on your lease and local law.

Two important distinctions:
- **If $850 is the full valid outstanding balance**, paying it may cure a payment default, subject to the lease’s cure provisions and any other defaults. I haven’t verified that amount.
- **“Under protest” does not automatically preserve every right**, invalidate the notice, or create a duty to issue a letter. Its effect varies by jurisdiction.

The best immediate approach is to seek a **written agreement exchanging the corrected payment for withdrawal of the notice and a signed no-default confirmation**. For example:

> Section 8.3 prohibits the compounded charges in your demand. My calculation of the properly due one-time late fees is $850. I am prepared to pay that amount promptly, without admitting liability for the disputed balance. Please confirm in writing that receipt will fully resolve the alleged payment default, that the remaining disputed charges will be removed, and that you will withdraw the notice dated [date] and provide a signed confirmation of no uncured default by [date/time before inspection].

**Don’t make a payment needed to meet an existing cure deadline conditional on their agreement without local legal advice.** A conditional tender might not count as an effective cure.

Today, confirm the board’s required wording and have a local commercial-lease attorney review the notice, cure clause, and any landlord certificate/estoppel provision. Those provisions may give you leverage to demand the document, but an enforceable right to a letter is not necessarily a way to obtain it before Tuesday.

What state or country is the property in, and what deadline does the default notice give you to cure?
